Assignment 6 – Energy-Based Model on MNIST¶

Akshu Karki

For this assignment I trained an energy-based model (EBM) on the MNIST handwritten digits. I started from the textbook code in notebooks/07_ebm/01_ebm/ebm.ipynb (Generative Deep Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 7) and made a few changes:

  • trained for 120 epochs instead of the 60 used in the book
  • small fixes so it runs on my setup (TensorFlow 2.20 / Keras 3)
  • saved the model at epoch 60 too, so I can compare the book's training length with mine on the same run
  • logged every metric to a CSV file so I could plot the loss curves at the end

The idea of an EBM is that the network gives every image a single number (a score). Real digits should get a high score and everything else a low score. The energy is just the negative of that score, so real digits = low energy. To generate new digits, we start from random noise and use Langevin dynamics: we keep moving the image a small step in the direction that increases the score (gradient ascent on the input) with a little bit of noise added each time.

0. Parameters¶

Same values as the book except for the number of epochs.

In [2]:
IMAGE_SIZE = 32
CHANNELS = 1
STEP_SIZE = 10
STEPS = 60
NOISE = 0.005
ALPHA = 0.1
GRADIENT_CLIP = 0.03
BATCH_SIZE = 128
BUFFER_SIZE = 8192
LEARNING_RATE = 0.0001
EPOCHS = 120

1. Load the data¶

MNIST has 60,000 training and 10,000 test images of size 28×28. Like the book, I scale the pixels to the range [-1, 1] and pad each image to 32×32 with the background value -1, so the image size works nicely with the stride-2 convolutions (32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2).

In [3]:
(x_train, _), (x_test, _) = datasets.mnist.load_data()


def preprocess(imgs):
    """
    Normalize and reshape the images
    """
    imgs = (imgs.astype("float32") - 127.5) / 127.5
    imgs = np.pad(imgs, ((0, 0), (2, 2), (2, 2)), constant_values=-1.0)
    imgs = np.expand_dims(imgs, -1)
    return imgs


x_train = preprocess(x_train)
x_test = preprocess(x_test)
print(x_train.shape, x_test.shape, x_train.min(), x_train.max())

x_train = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(x_train).batch(BATCH_SIZE)
x_test = tf.data.Dataset.from_tensor_slices(x_test).batch(BATCH_SIZE)

2. Build the energy function network¶

This is the network that represents the energy function E(x). It takes a 32×32 image and outputs one number. It's four Conv2D layers with stride 2 (each one halves the image size) and swish activations, then a Dense(64) layer and a final Dense(1) with no activation, because the score can be any real number.

The book uses swish instead of ReLU because the Langevin sampler needs the gradient of the output with respect to the input image. Swish is smooth, so the gradients are smooth too, while ReLU gradients jump between 0 and 1.

In [5]:
ebm_input = layers.Input(shape=(IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS))
x = layers.Conv2D(
    16, kernel_size=5, strides=2, padding="same", activation=activations.swish
)(ebm_input)
x = layers.Conv2D(
    32, kernel_size=3, strides=2, padding="same", activation=activations.swish
)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(
    64, kernel_size=3, strides=2, padding="same", activation=activations.swish
)(x)
x = layers.Conv2D(
    64, kernel_size=3, strides=2, padding="same", activation=activations.swish
)(x)
x = layers.Flatten()(x)
x = layers.Dense(64, activation=activations.swish)(x)
ebm_output = layers.Dense(1)(x)
model = models.Model(ebm_input, ebm_output)
model.summary()

3. Langevin sampler¶

This function is how the EBM makes new images. For each step it:

  1. adds a small amount of Gaussian noise to the images
  2. computes the gradient of the score with respect to the input pixels (not the weights)
  3. clips the gradient to ±0.03 so one step can't change the image too much
  4. moves the image step_size times the gradient in the direction that increases the score

The math is exactly the same as the book. The only change is that I moved one Langevin step into its own function with @tf.function. Every training batch runs 60 of these steps, and in eager mode the first epoch took about 5 minutes, which would have been around 10 hours for 120 epochs. Compiling just this one step brought it down to under 2 minutes per epoch without changing what the code does.

In [6]:
@tf.function
def langevin_step(model, inp_imgs, step_size, noise):
    inp_imgs += tf.random.normal(tf.shape(inp_imgs), mean=0, stddev=noise)
    inp_imgs = tf.clip_by_value(inp_imgs, -1.0, 1.0)
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        tape.watch(inp_imgs)
        out_score = model(inp_imgs)
    grads = tape.gradient(out_score, inp_imgs)
    grads = tf.clip_by_value(grads, -GRADIENT_CLIP, GRADIENT_CLIP)
    inp_imgs += step_size * grads
    inp_imgs = tf.clip_by_value(inp_imgs, -1.0, 1.0)
    return inp_imgs


def generate_samples(
    model, inp_imgs, steps, step_size, noise, return_img_per_step=False
):
    inp_imgs = tf.convert_to_tensor(inp_imgs, dtype=tf.float32)
    imgs_per_step = []
    for _ in range(steps):
        inp_imgs = langevin_step(model, inp_imgs, float(step_size), float(noise))
        if return_img_per_step:
            imgs_per_step.append(inp_imgs)
    if return_img_per_step:
        return tf.stack(imgs_per_step, axis=0)
    else:
        return inp_imgs

4. Replay buffer¶

Running Langevin from pure noise every batch would need hundreds of steps. Instead, the book keeps a buffer of up to 8,192 fake images from earlier batches. Each batch, about 95% of the starting images come from the buffer and about 5% are fresh random noise, and then only 60 Langevin steps are run. The new fakes go back into the buffer. This is the "persistent" version of contrastive divergence.

In [7]:
class Buffer:
    def __init__(self, model):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model
        self.examples = [
            tf.random.uniform(shape=(1, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS)) * 2
            - 1
            for _ in range(BATCH_SIZE)
        ]

    def sample_new_exmps(self, steps, step_size, noise):
        n_new = np.random.binomial(BATCH_SIZE, 0.05)
        rand_imgs = (
            tf.random.uniform((n_new, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS)) * 2 - 1
        )
        old_imgs = tf.concat(
            random.choices(self.examples, k=BATCH_SIZE - n_new), axis=0
        )
        inp_imgs = tf.concat([rand_imgs, old_imgs], axis=0)
        inp_imgs = generate_samples(
            self.model, inp_imgs, steps=steps, step_size=step_size, noise=noise
        )
        self.examples = tf.split(inp_imgs, BATCH_SIZE, axis=0) + self.examples
        self.examples = self.examples[:BUFFER_SIZE]
        return inp_imgs

5. Custom Keras model with the contrastive divergence training step¶

This is the main part of the assignment. train_step does one step of contrastive divergence:

  1. add a tiny bit of noise to the real images (helps the sampler, same as the book)
  2. get fake images from the buffer + 60 Langevin steps
  3. pass real and fake images through the network together and split the scores
  4. contrastive divergence loss = mean(fake score) − mean(real score). Minimizing this pushes real scores up and fake scores down (so real images get low energy and fakes get high energy).
  5. regularization loss = α · mean(real² + fake²) with α = 0.1. Without this, the network could just make the scores huge and the loss would go to −∞.
  6. update the weights with Adam

test_step is from the book too. It compares real test images against pure uniform noise (no Langevin), so it shows if the model can tell digits apart from random noise.

The only change from the book: in Keras 3 the metrics property needs to be defined like this to reset each epoch, which the book already does, so the class didn't need changes.

In [8]:
class EBM(models.Model):
    def __init__(self):
        super(EBM, self).__init__()
        self.model = model
        self.buffer = Buffer(self.model)
        self.alpha = ALPHA
        self.loss_metric = metrics.Mean(name="loss")
        self.reg_loss_metric = metrics.Mean(name="reg")
        self.cdiv_loss_metric = metrics.Mean(name="cdiv")
        self.real_out_metric = metrics.Mean(name="real")
        self.fake_out_metric = metrics.Mean(name="fake")

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [
            self.loss_metric,
            self.reg_loss_metric,
            self.cdiv_loss_metric,
            self.real_out_metric,
            self.fake_out_metric,
        ]

    def train_step(self, real_imgs):
        real_imgs += tf.random.normal(
            shape=tf.shape(real_imgs), mean=0, stddev=NOISE
        )
        real_imgs = tf.clip_by_value(real_imgs, -1.0, 1.0)
        fake_imgs = self.buffer.sample_new_exmps(
            steps=STEPS, step_size=STEP_SIZE, noise=NOISE
        )
        inp_imgs = tf.concat([real_imgs, fake_imgs], axis=0)
        with tf.GradientTape() as training_tape:
            real_out, fake_out = tf.split(self.model(inp_imgs), 2, axis=0)
            cdiv_loss = tf.reduce_mean(fake_out, axis=0) - tf.reduce_mean(
                real_out, axis=0
            )
            reg_loss = self.alpha * tf.reduce_mean(
                real_out**2 + fake_out**2, axis=0
            )
            loss = cdiv_loss + reg_loss
        grads = training_tape.gradient(loss, self.model.trainable_variables)
        self.optimizer.apply_gradients(
            zip(grads, self.model.trainable_variables)
        )
        self.loss_metric.update_state(loss)
        self.reg_loss_metric.update_state(reg_loss)
        self.cdiv_loss_metric.update_state(cdiv_loss)
        self.real_out_metric.update_state(tf.reduce_mean(real_out, axis=0))
        self.fake_out_metric.update_state(tf.reduce_mean(fake_out, axis=0))
        return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics}

    def test_step(self, real_imgs):
        batch_size = real_imgs.shape[0]
        fake_imgs = (
            tf.random.uniform((batch_size, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS))
            * 2
            - 1
        )
        inp_imgs = tf.concat([real_imgs, fake_imgs], axis=0)
        real_out, fake_out = tf.split(self.model(inp_imgs), 2, axis=0)
        cdiv = tf.reduce_mean(fake_out, axis=0) - tf.reduce_mean(
            real_out, axis=0
        )
        self.cdiv_loss_metric.update_state(cdiv)
        self.real_out_metric.update_state(tf.reduce_mean(real_out, axis=0))
        self.fake_out_metric.update_state(tf.reduce_mean(fake_out, axis=0))
        return {m.name: m.result() for m in self.metrics[2:]}


ebm = EBM()

6. Train for 120 epochs¶

Adam with learning rate 1e-4, same as the book. Like the book, I use run_eagerly=True because the buffer uses normal Python lists and random.choices, which don't work inside a compiled TensorFlow graph. The slow part (the Langevin steps) is already compiled from section 3, so the training step itself can stay exactly like the book.

Callbacks:

  • ImageGenerator – the book makes 10 new digits from noise (1000 Langevin steps) after every epoch. With 120 epochs that's too many plots, so I save a picture every 10 epochs and only show epochs 1, 60 and 120 here.
  • SaveModel – saves the weights every epoch, plus an extra copy at epoch 60 (where the book stops). Keras 3 needs the file name to end in .weights.h5.
  • CSVLogger – writes all the metrics to output/training_log.csv after every epoch.
  • PrintLoss – prints a short summary every 10 epochs so the output isn't 120 progress bars.
In [9]:
ebm.compile(
    optimizer=optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE), run_eagerly=True
)


class ImageGenerator(callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, num_img, every=10, show_at=(1, 60, 120)):
        self.num_img = num_img
        self.every = every
        self.show_at = show_at

    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        e = epoch + 1
        if e != 1 and e % self.every != 0:
            return
        start_imgs = (
            np.random.uniform(
                size=(self.num_img, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS)
            )
            * 2
            - 1
        )
        generated_images = generate_samples(
            ebm.model,
            start_imgs,
            steps=1000,
            step_size=STEP_SIZE,
            noise=NOISE,
            return_img_per_step=False,
        ).numpy()
        example_images = tf.concat(
            random.choices(ebm.buffer.examples, k=10), axis=0
        ).numpy()
        if e in self.show_at:
            print(f"Epoch {e}: new digits from noise (top), buffer examples (bottom)")
            display(generated_images, save_to="./output/generated_img_%03d.png" % e)
            display(example_images, save_to="./output/example_img_%03d.png" % e)
        else:
            for imgs, name in [(generated_images, "generated"), (example_images, "example")]:
                plt.figure(figsize=(20, 3))
                for i in range(10):
                    plt.subplot(1, 10, i + 1)
                    plt.imshow((imgs[i] + 1) / 2, cmap="gray_r")
                    plt.axis("off")
                plt.savefig("./output/%s_img_%03d.png" % (name, e))
                plt.close()


class SaveModel(callbacks.Callback):
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        model.save_weights("./models/model.weights.h5")
        if epoch + 1 == 60:
            model.save_weights("./models/model_epoch060.weights.h5")


class PrintLoss(callbacks.Callback):
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        e = epoch + 1
        if e == 1 or e % 10 == 0:
            print(
                f"epoch {e:>3}: loss={logs['loss']:.4f}  cdiv={logs['cdiv']:.4f}  "
                f"reg={logs['reg']:.4f}  real={logs['real']:.3f}  fake={logs['fake']:.3f}  "
                f"val_cdiv={logs['val_cdiv']:.3f}",
                flush=True,
            )


image_generator_callback = ImageGenerator(num_img=10)
csv_logger = callbacks.CSVLogger("./output/training_log.csv")
In [10]:
history = ebm.fit(
    x_train,
    shuffle=True,
    epochs=EPOCHS,
    validation_data=x_test,
    callbacks=[
        SaveModel(),
        csv_logger,
        image_generator_callback,
        PrintLoss(),
    ],
    verbose=0,
)

7. Loss curves¶

I plot four things from the training log:

  • the total loss (contrastive divergence + regularization), which is what the optimizer actually minimizes
  • the two parts of the loss separately
  • the average score the network gives to real images vs. fake (Langevin) images
  • the validation contrastive divergence (real test digits vs. pure noise)
In [11]:
log = pd.read_csv("./output/training_log.csv")
ep = log["epoch"] + 1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 9))

axes[0, 0].plot(ep, log["loss"], color="tab:blue")

axes[0, 0].set(title="Total training loss (cdiv + reg)", xlabel="Epoch", ylabel="Loss")

axes[0, 1].plot(ep, log["cdiv"], label="contrastive divergence")
axes[0, 1].plot(ep, log["reg"], label="regularization")

8. Generate new digits¶

Now I make 10 new digits starting from uniform noise with 1000 Langevin steps, the same way as the book. To compare fairly, I use the same starting noise for the epoch 60 model (the book's training length) and the epoch 120 model.

In [12]:

    np.random.uniform(size=(10, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS)) * 2 - 1
).astype("float32")

    model, tf.constant(start_imgs), steps=1000, step_size=STEP_SIZE,
    noise=NOISE, return_img_per_step=True,
)

model.load_weights("./models/model.weights.h5")

Sanity check¶

To check that the energy function actually learned something, I compare the average score the final model gives to:

  • real test digits
  • pure uniform noise
  • the 10 digits I just generated

If the model works, real digits and generated digits should score much higher (lower energy) than noise.

In [14]:
real_scores = np.concatenate([model(b).numpy().ravel() for b in x_test])
noise_scores = model(
    tf.random.uniform((10000, IMAGE_SIZE, IMAGE_SIZE, CHANNELS)) * 2 - 1
).numpy().ravel()
gen_scores = model(gen_120[-1]).numpy().ravel()

print(f"real test digits : mean score {real_scores.mean():8.3f}   (energy {-real_scores.mean():8.3f})")
print(f"uniform noise    : mean score {noise_scores.mean():8.3f}   (energy {-noise_scores.mean():8.3f})")
print(f"generated digits : mean score {gen_scores.mean():8.3f}   (energy {-gen_scores.mean():8.3f})")

10. Results and comparison with the book¶

Loss curve¶

The loss curve for an EBM looks really different from the other models we trained. With RealNVP the loss went down smoothly, but here the total loss sits at basically 0 for the first 84 epochs (for example −0.039 at epoch 1, 0.0003 at epoch 10, −0.0001 at epoch 60). At first I thought this meant nothing was being learned, but that's not it. The contrastive divergence loss is mean(fake score) − mean(real score), and the buffer fakes keep getting better at the same time as the network. So the real and fake scores both stay around 0 and cancel out, and the regularization term (α = 0.1) keeps them from drifting. A loss near 0 actually means the sampler is keeping up with the network, which is what you want.

The learning shows up in the other plots instead:

  • the validation cdiv (real test digits vs. pure noise) drops from −1.47 at epoch 1 to −26.1 at epoch 60 and reaches its lowest value, −29.0 at epoch 69. So the network gets better and better at giving digits low energy and noise high energy.
  • the generated digits get better: blotches at epoch 1, digit-like strokes at epoch 10, real digits by epoch 20–40 (but lots of 5s), and clean, varied digits (0 to 9) at epochs 60–80.

What happened after epoch 84¶

At epoch 85 the training suddenly changed. In about 8 epochs the real score went from 0 to +4.8 and the fake score went to −4.8, so the total loss dropped from 0 to about −5 and stayed there until epoch 120 (lowest −4.995 at epoch 106). −5 is actually the smallest value this loss can reach: if real = r and fake = −r, the loss is −2r + 0.1·2r², which is smallest at r = 5, giving −5. So the model ended up at the exact minimum of the loss, but this is a bad sign, not a good one.

The images explain why. From epoch 90 on, every generated image is the same dark blob, and 9 out of 10 buffer images at epoch 90 are that blob too. My understanding of what happened:

  1. at some point the Langevin sampler found a spot in image space that the network scored highly, even though it isn't a digit
  2. because the buffer keeps recycling old fakes, that pattern quickly spread through most of the buffer
  3. once almost all the fakes were the same blob, it was really easy for the network to tell them apart from real digits, so it pushed real up to +5 and fakes down to −5
  4. now the network learns nothing useful about what digits look like, and starting from noise the sampler just walks back into the same blob (you can see this in the step-by-step plot in section 8)

The final scores in section 9 confirm it. The epoch 60 model gives real digits and its generated digits almost the same score (0.007 vs. 0.044), and 7 of 10 generated images score at least as high as an average real digit. The epoch 120 model gives real digits 4.93 but its own samples −4.72, and 0 of 10 samples score like real digits. So the final model can recognize digits but can't generate them anymore. EBM training is known to be unstable like this, because the network and the sampler are trained against each other (Du & Mordatch, 2019).

Comparing with the book¶

My code is the book's code (same network, same Langevin sampler, same buffer, same contrastive divergence training step and the same hyperparameters). The only differences are the number of epochs and that I compiled one Langevin step with @tf.function to make it faster. So my epoch 60 model is what the book's setup gives.

  • At 60 epochs my results match the book. The book shows that starting from random noise and running 1000 Langevin steps produces new images that clearly look like MNIST digits, and that a single image slowly turns from noise into a digit during sampling. My epoch 60 model does the same thing: clean digits like 2, 1, 7, 9 and 0, and in the step-by-step plot the noise first fades into a faint shape and then turns into a "1" by step 300–999.
  • Training for 120 epochs made it worse, not better. The digits kept improving until about epoch 80, but then training collapsed at epoch 85 and the final model only produces the same noisy blob. With RealNVP in Assignment 5, extra epochs didn't help much but didn't hurt either. Here they actually broke the model.
  • The lowest loss was not the best model. The loss was lowest after the collapse (−4.99), when the samples were useless. For an EBM the loss value can't be used to pick the best epoch. You have to look at the samples, or at the scores of the generated images vs. real ones.

What I would change next time¶

  • save a checkpoint every 10 epochs and keep the one with the best samples (in this run that would have been around epoch 70–80), or stop early when the real and fake scores start to split apart
  • watch how varied the buffer is, since it filling up with the same image was the first warning sign
  • try a smaller learning rate or a larger regularization α for the second half of training, to make the jump at epoch 85 less likely
  • run it again with a different random seed. This was a single run, so the collapse could happen earlier, later, or not at all with another seed.

Reference¶

Du, Y., & Mordatch, I. (2019). Implicit generation and generalization in energy-based models. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 32. https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.08689

Foster, D. (2023). Generative deep learning: Teaching machines to paint, write, compose, and play (2nd ed.). O'Reilly Media.
